name: Bulgaria
summary_text: Bulgaria is workable for trans visitors — an EU member with no traveler-facing restrictions, but one of the EU's most hostile social climates. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The European Court of Justice is actively hearing the Shipov case on Bulgaria's refusal to issue ID matching lived gender, and EU free-movement law provides a legal backstop. The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the Supreme Court of Cassation ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (gender an "unchangeable biological factor"), parliament passed a Russia-style law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools (August 2024), and the EU's FRA survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above EU averages. Hate speech by politicians is routine. For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and Sofia has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.

sources.claim_summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Bulgaria: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by Vazrazhdane leader Kostadinov); Bulgaria continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from Russia and Belarus and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from Palestine in closed detention; a Sofia Pride performer received death threats; a LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

sources.title: Bulgaria | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But Article 46 of the constitution bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. Koilova and Babulkova v. Bulgaria (ECtHR 2023) found Bulgaria in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III country sheet for Bulgaria (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU-27: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU-27: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

sources.title: Bulgaria asked to recognize trans' 'lived gender identity'
sources.claim_summary: DW (Sept 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued a non-binding opinion that Bulgaria must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the Shipov case, concerning a Bulgarian trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the Court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

sources.title: Ban on legal gender recognition: the missed opportunity of the Y.T. v Bulgaria revision - Strasbourg Observers
sources.claim_summary: Strasbourg Observers analysis (Dec 2024) of Y.T. v. Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of rights, but the Court confirmed Bulgaria remains obliged under Article 8 (per P.H. v. Bulgaria) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which Bulgaria still lacks.

sources.title: Bulgaria must investigate and prosecute hate crimes to end climate of fear - Amnesty International
sources.claim_summary: Amnesty International report (Feb 2015): 'Missing the point' - Bulgaria's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, Muslims and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.

sources.title: Sofia LGBT Pride Should Showcase a Tolerant Bulgaria | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch (Jun 2017): 'Sofia LGBT Pride Should Showcase a Tolerant Bulgaria' — op-ed urging authorities to protect Sofia Pride and show a tolerant face.
Novinite (June 2011): the 4th Sofia Pride passed without incidents under heavy police guard - after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 parades; only a 'family NGO' protested.
